quote: Natural selection would have quickly eliminated brains so completely unsuited to reasoning, so anti-helpful, as anti-Occamian or anti-Laplacian priors.
content: Selection rewards fitness, not accuracy, and where the two part ways it favors systematic error. Error-management theory predicts biased inference wherever false alarms and misses carry unequal costs, and finds it (Haselton & Buss 2000). In simulations of how perception evolves, strategies tuned to fitness payoffs drive truth-tracking strategies to extinction (Hoffman, Singh & Prakash 2015). Selection would eliminate priors that kill. It would not eliminate a prior that is badly wrong about things irrelevant to reproduction, such as cosmology or the foundations of mathematics. Book III spent many pages on how badly evolved minds reason off the savanna, and this argument asks us to trust that same process to have installed the right inductive foundations.

quote: Which would violate the Second Law of Thermodynamics by generating information from nowhere.
content: Believing a false sentence creates no physical information and breaks no law of thermodynamics. The Second Law is about the entropy of physical systems, not about whether beliefs are warranted. Had the paper stated the true mass of helium, believing it on the paper's say-so would be just as unjustified and just as thermodynamically innocent. The appeal to physics dresses up an epistemological point (self-certification is not evidence) in a law that has nothing to say about it. Book IV repeats the habit in "The Second Law of Thermodynamics, and Engines of Cognition."

quote: Ah, but we evolved by natural selection; we were not generated randomly.
content: This is the step the "easy knowledge" literature was built to examine. We know we evolved by natural selection through empirical science, done with the same inductive faculties whose reliability is in question. Using that result to vouch for those faculties is bootstrapping, the kind that Vogel (2000) and Cohen (2002) argue would let any method certify itself. A believer can tell a story with the identical structure: God made our faculties, so they are reliable. Plantinga built reformed epistemology on that symmetry. The essay's "reflective loop" is legitimate only if it can be told apart from these, and the essay never says how.

quote: if it had not said that grasshoppers had four legs
content: Leviticus doesn't say grasshoppers have four legs. Leviticus 11:20 forbids "all winged swarming things that go upon all fours," an idiom for creeping along the ground. Verse 11:21 immediately exempts those "which have jointed legs above their feet, with which to leap upon the earth," and the next verse names locusts, crickets and grasshoppers as permitted. The text singles out the leaping hind legs, which is the opposite of a miscount. A book that judges a source's reliability by its errors should get the error right.

quote: I do think that reflective loops have a meta-character which should enable one to distinguish them, by common sense, from circular logics.
content: Here the essay admits its central distinction has no criterion except "common sense." Common sense is the one thing it can't rest on, because the believer it argues against also judges by common sense that his own loop is reflective and the atheist's is vicious. There is a real literature on justifying inference rules by circular arguments, and it offers candidate criteria: Braithwaite, Black (1958), and Van Cleve (1984), who defends an inductive justification of induction. It also contains the standard objection. Salmon (1957) showed that counter-induction can be "justified" counter-inductively by exactly the same structure. The anti-Laplacian minds earlier in this essay are Salmon's objection, played as a joke instead of answered.
